lesson.title: Splitting the Difference: Electrons Held in Common
lesson.summary: Covalent bonds form when two atoms share one or more pairs of valence electrons rather than transferring them outright, and how many pairs they share directly determines how strong and how short the resulting bond is.
lesson.body:
Where an ionic bond resolves the competition for valence electrons by handing them entirely to one atom, a covalent bond resolves it by compromise: two atoms each contribute one or more valence electrons to a shared pair that both nuclei attract simultaneously. This tends to happen between atoms with similar electronegativities, most often two nonmetals, since neither atom has enough of an advantage to strip the electron away from the other. The shared pair sits in the region of overlap between the two atoms' valence orbitals, and it is attracted to both positively charged nuclei at once, which is exactly the source of the lowered potential energy that makes bonding favorable in the first place.

The number of electron pairs shared between two atoms is called the bond order, and it has a direct, measurable effect on bond strength and bond length. A single bond shares one pair, a double bond shares two pairs, and a triple bond shares three pairs. More shared pairs means more electron density pulling the two nuclei together, so bond energy rises and bond length shrinks as bond order increases. Carbon to carbon bonds show this cleanly: a single carbon to carbon bond has a bond energy of roughly 347 kilojoules per mole, a double bond rises to about 614 kilojoules per mole, and a triple bond climbs to about 839 kilojoules per mole, with the bond getting measurably shorter at each step. Nitrogen gas, N2, is held together by an unusually strong triple bond, about 945 kilojoules per mole, which is exactly why N2 is so chemically unreactive despite being the largest single component of the atmosphere: breaking that bond simply costs too much energy for most reactions to supply.

Covalent bonds are rarely perfectly even, and this is where electronegativity comes back into the picture directly. When two identical atoms bond, as in Cl2 or H2, the electronegativity difference is exactly zero, the shared pair sits exactly midway between the nuclei, and the bond is nonpolar covalent. When the bonded atoms differ in electronegativity, as in hydrogen chloride, where hydrogen sits at 2.20 and chlorine at 3.16, the shared pair is pulled statistically closer to the more electronegative atom, giving chlorine a partial negative charge and hydrogen a partial positive charge without any electron being fully transferred. This is called a polar covalent bond, and it is best understood as sitting on a continuum between the perfectly even sharing of a nonpolar covalent bond and the essentially complete transfer of an ionic bond, with the electronegativity difference between the two atoms determining where on that continuum a given bond falls.

Covalent bonding is also what allows atoms to build up the complex, discrete molecules that make up most of organic chemistry and biochemistry, in contrast to the extended, repeating networks that ionic bonding tends to produce. A single water molecule, H2O, or a single glucose molecule exists as its own defined unit held together by covalent bonds, with a specific number of atoms and a specific shape, and that molecule can exist as a gas, dissolved in a liquid, or packed into a solid without changing its fundamental covalent framework. This molecular character is one of the clearest practical distinctions between covalent bonding and the ionic bonding covered previously, and it sets up the third major bonding category, metallic bonding, where valence electrons are shared not just between two atoms but across an entire sample all at once.
